strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: reframing group-based advantage computation as estimating a Bernoulli reward probability, and using a discounted Beta–Bernoulli posterior mean in place of the empirical mean. This costs essentially no extra compute or memory, unlike replay-based alternatives.

The statistical analysis is correct and clearly presented. The observation that H_τ is deterministic given N and λ (Appendix B.1), which cleanly separates the stochastic part of the estimator, is a nice technical touch, and the bias–variance decomposition (Eqs. 17–19, 36–37) is carefully derived.

The paper claims and demonstrates avoidance of variance collapse at the estimator level: the posterior variance α_τβ_τ/(α_τ+β_τ)^2 is strictly positive, in contrast to the empirical variance which is zero when all rollouts in a group receive identical rewards.

Empirical evaluation is fairly broad: two model scales (1.7B/8B), six in-distribution and three out-of-distribution benchmarks, a replay-based baseline (RePO), an ablation over λ (Table 2), a direct empirical MSE analysis using 128 extra rollouts as a reference (Fig. 3), and a demonstration that DBB also improves Dr.GRPO (Table 3), supporting generality beyond one algorithm.

The MSE analysis (Section 5.3) is a valuable addition: it directly connects estimator accuracy (minimized near λ=0.4) to downstream performance (best at λ=0.5), rather than relying only on benchmark numbers.
weaknesses: A key experimental confound: GRPO-DBB is trained with a different clipping range (0.98, 0.98) than all baselines (0.2, 0.28 with clip-higher). Appendix C justifies this only briefly. This is a material change to the training objective, and the paper does not disentangle how much of the reported gain comes from DBB versus the modified clipping configuration. A baseline with DBB and the standard clipping range, or GRPO with the DBB clipping range, is needed.

No variance across random seeds is reported. Several per-benchmark gains are small (e.g., +0.23 on Minerva, +0.87 on MATH500 for the 8B model) and could plausibly fall within seed-to-seed noise; only averages of 2–3 points are clearly above plausible noise levels.

The theoretical framework assumes reward probabilities evolve gradually across epochs (bias term Σ c_k(p_k − p_τ)). This assumption is unverified in general: between two visits to the same prompt (separated by a full epoch), the policy may have changed substantially, and the amount of history available is bounded by the number of epochs (4 here). The method's applicability to single-pass training over large datasets is not discussed.

The exact advantage computation with DBB is under-specified in the main text: Algorithm 1 says 'Compute advantage Â_i with (α_τ, β_τ) and X_i' but it is unclear whether the normalizer σ in Eq. (2) is replaced by the model variance in Eq. (13), the estimator variance, or something else. This is central to the method and hurts reproducibility as written.

Novelty is modest. Discounted Bayesian/conjugate updating of a Bernoulli parameter is textbook material (equivalent to an exponentially weighted moving average with a prior), and the contribution is primarily an application of this standard estimator to GRPO advantage computation. The framing of this as a new 'statistical estimation perspective' overstates the technical advance somewhat.

OOD benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA-D, BBH) are evaluated only on 'the best checkpoint selected for each experiment,' and λ was selected using validation performance; combined with the single-run setup, the large OOD gains (up to +21 points on BBH) carry extra selection uncertainty.

Fairness of the RePO comparison is questionable: RePO was trained on 8×H200 GPUs at both scales while other methods used 4 for the 1.7B model, and hyperparameters were taken from the original paper, so compute-normalized comparison is not exact.

Presentation has noticeable typos and errors: 'HBB estimation' in Section 4, 'p̂_τ^db' vs 'p̂_τ^dbb' inconsistency, 'we make the estimator's dependence on...' (Section 3.3 sentence is broken), and Section 5.4 refers to 'Figure 2(b)' when reporting the MSE-vs-N result that is actually Figure 3(b). No code release is stated.
Only one replay baseline and one training dataset are used; robustness of the gains beyond DAPO-Math-17k and beyond math-style RLVR is untested.

strengths: The core idea is simple, well-motivated, and practical: recasting GRPO's group-mean advantage computation as low-sample estimation of a per-prompt Bernoulli parameter and applying a discounted (exponentially weighted) Beta-Bernoulli posterior adds essentially no compute or memory overhead, in contrast to replay-based alternatives like RePO.

The statistical analysis is transparent and honest: the paper explicitly acknowledges that DBB is biased, derives its expectation, variance, and MSE under non-stationarity (Appendix B), and clearly contrasts it with the unbiased but high-variance point estimator. The framing of variance collapse as an estimation artifact is a useful perspective.

The empirical evaluation is broad: two model scales (Qwen3-1.7B/8B-Base), six in-distribution and three OOD benchmarks, ablations on the discount factor λ (Table 2), an empirical MSE analysis connecting estimation accuracy to downstream performance (Figure 3, Section 5.3), and a demonstration of generality via Dr.GRPO-DBB (Table 3). The alignment between the λ that minimizes MSE and the λ that yields best accuracy is a nice supporting observation.
Training dynamics analysis (Section 5.1, Figure 2) offers some mechanistic insight, e.g., controlled entropy growth and response-length behavior under DBB versus GRPO.
weaknesses: A potentially serious experimental confound: the appendix states that DBB uses a different, much wider clipping range (0.98, 0.98) than all baselines (0.2, 0.28), justified only informally by 'larger importance ratios'. This is a substantial hyperparameter change that is never ablated, so the reported gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the DBB estimator rather than to the clipping modification. A GRPO + (0.98, 0.98) baseline without DBB is required to support the central claim.

The claimed mechanism for avoiding variance collapse is under-examined. When all N rewards in a group are identical (the zero-variance case), the DBB advantage is driven by the biased stale-history term w(μ_{τ-1} − p_τ), i.e., it injects a nonzero training signal from outdated information. The paper frames this as 'preserving informative signals' but provides no analysis or experiment isolating whether this injected stale signal helps or hurts; the theoretical guarantees concern estimating p_τ, not the quality or correctness of the resulting policy gradient.

The theory rests on strong modeling assumptions that are not validated: i.i.d. Bernoulli rollouts per prompt per epoch, independence across epochs, and a quasi-stationarity assumption ({p_k} close to p_τ) that is explicitly violated early in training. Moreover, no general theorem is given that DBB's MSE is lower than the point estimator's — this is only shown empirically for specific λ, N, and one model scale (Figure 3), so the abstract's 'achieves lower mean squared error than standard point estimation' is overclaimed as a general result.

No statistical significance assessment: results are based on a single training run per configuration with no seeds or error bars, yet headline claims rest on differences of a few points on very small benchmarks (AIME24/25 have ~30 problems each; Acc@8 granularity is coarse). The very large OOD gains (e.g., +21.26 on BBH for 1.7B) relative to in-distribution gains are surprising and unexplained, and evaluations on OlympiadBench and all OOD benchmarks were performed only on the 'best checkpoint selected for each experiment,' which adds selection variance and weakens confidence.

Modest originality: discounted/forgetting Bayesian shrinkage (EWMA-style conjugate updates) is textbook material; the contribution is its application to GRPO reward estimation. The per-model empirical tuning of λ (0.5 vs 0.75) with only retrospective interpretation via training-reward dynamics provides no principled selection rule for practitioners.

Presentation issues undermine polish: 'HBB estimation' typo in Section 4 opening, an incomplete sentence in Section 3.3 ('To make the estimator's dependence on the underlying reward probabilities {p1,...,pτ}, we re-express...'), inconsistent dataset naming ('DAPO 17k' vs 'DAPO-Math-17k'), and the empirical MSE 'ground truth' itself uses a noisy 128-rollout surrogate whose error is not quantified.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters and setups are documented, but there is no code release mentioned, and the interaction between DBB and the modified clipping makes exact replication of the reported gains difficult without the missing ablation.

strengths: The core idea is clean and practical: recasting group-based advantage computation as reward-distribution estimation and replacing the empirical mean with a discounted Beta–Bernoulli posterior mean. This is easy to implement, adds no memory or forward-pass overhead, and is a genuinely underexplored angle relative to rollout-side fixes (dynamic sampling, selective rollout) and replay-based methods.

The statistical analysis is correct and clearly presented. The bias–variance decomposition (Eqs. 14–15), the unrolled weighted-average form (Eq. 31), and the conditional MSE in Appendix B are straightforward but rigorously derived, and Table 4 is a helpful summary.

The paper honestly frames DBB as a biased estimator and supports the central mechanism with a dedicated empirical MSE analysis (Section 5.3), showing the MSE-optimal λ (≈0.4) aligns with the λ that performs best downstream — a nice link between estimation quality and RL performance.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: two model scales, six in-distribution and three OOD benchmarks, a λ ablation (Table 2), and a generality check on Dr.GRPO (Table 3) showing the idea is not GRPO-specific.
Training-dynamics analysis (Figure 2) offers qualitative insight into why DBB helps (longer responses, controlled entropy).
weaknesses: The headline theoretical claim is weaker than stated. The abstract says the estimator 'achieves lower mean squared error than standard point estimation,' but the theory only derives the MSE expressions; no theorem establishes MSE(dbb) < MSE(pt) for any nontrivial regime. The comparison is purely empirical (Figure 3). Similarly, 'theoretically avoids variance collapse' concerns the posterior variance estimate, and the paper does not formally connect avoiding variance collapse to policy improvement.

The advantage construction with (ατ, βτ) is underspecified. Algorithm 1 line 11 says 'Compute advantage Âi with (ατ, βτ) and Xi' but the main text never states the exact formula (is Âi = (Xi − p̂dbb)/posterior-std? posterior-std or Var estimate of Eq. 13?). This is the actual quantity fed to the clipped objective and is essential for reproducibility.

A significant experimental confound: GRPO-DBB uses a different clipping range (0.98, 0.98) than all baselines (0.2, 0.28). The authors justify this by the larger importance ratios under DBB, which itself indicates DBB changes the optimization dynamics well beyond reward estimation. The reported gains therefore cannot be attributed cleanly to the estimator alone; an ablation with matched clipping is needed. The notation (0.98, 0.98) also appears inconsistent/possibly erroneous relative to the (0.2, 0.28) convention and needs clarification.

No error bars, seeds, or significance tests anywhere. Several deltas are small (e.g., +0.23 on Minerva for 8B) and benchmarks like AIME24/25 have ~30 problems, where Acc@8 differences of a few points can easily be noise. The consistently positive pattern mitigates this, but single-run comparisons cannot support the claim of uniform superiority on every benchmark.

Hyperparameter and checkpoint selection risks inflating results: λ is chosen per model from downstream performance trends (Section 5.2), the validation set overlaps the evaluation benchmarks, and OOD/OlympiadBench evaluation is performed only on 'the best checkpoint selected for each experiment' (Appendix C). This selection procedure is not applied symmetrically or described precisely enough to rule out bias favoring DBB.

Missing key baselines for the variance-collapse problem the paper targets. DAPO-style dynamic sampling is discussed as motivation but not compared against, so the claim that DBB addresses variance collapse more efficiently is not directly tested.

The theory assumes i.i.d. rollouts from the current policy per epoch and treats historical rewards as drawn from a drifting Bernoulli parameter per prompt, but the bias term depends on |pk − pτ|, whose magnitude is never analyzed or bounded — only argued qualitatively to be small when learning is 'gradual.' The off-policy nature of reusing historical rewards is handled heuristically via discounting without formal justification.
Novelty is modest: exponential forgetting + Beta–Bernoulli conjugacy is standard Bayesian machinery; the contribution is its application to GRPO advantage estimation. Useful, but incremental.
Presentation issues: 'HBB estimation' typo in Section 4, inconsistent notation p̂db vs p̂dbb, and Figure 3(b) referred to as 'Figure 2(b)' in Section 5.3.
No code release or mention of one, which limits reproducibility given the underspecified advantage computation and nonstandard clipping setup.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing of group-based RLVR advantage computation as a statistical estimation problem, with a simple, memory-free method (discounted Beta-Bernoulli posterior per prompt) that requires no extra rollouts or forward passes.

The theoretical analysis (Eqs. 14-20, Appendix B) is correct and transparent: the estimator's expectation, variance, and MSE are derived in closed form under non-stationary rewards, and the bias-variance/shrinkage interpretation is intuitive.

Extensive and careful empirical evaluation: two model scales (plus a 0.6B ablation), six in-distribution and three OOD benchmarks, four baselines (GRPO, RePO, GRESO, DAPO), standardized total rollout budgets, four independent runs with paired t-tests and reported p-values.

Notably honest and thorough ablation work: discount factor λ sweeps with a coherent explanation of scale-dependent optimal λ, prior sensitivity analysis (Appendix E), Best@8 analysis (Appendix F), comparisons against EMA/Laplace/empirical-Bayes shrinkage alternatives (Appendices H-I), and a dedicated control experiment isolating the effect of the wider clipping range used for GRPO-DBB (Appendix D).

The proposed estimator directly addresses variance collapse at the estimator level, and the training-dynamics analysis (entropy, response length, zero-variance prompt handling) offers a plausible mechanistic account of the gains.
weaknesses: The exact advantage formula used by GRPO-DBB is never fully specified in the main text: Algorithm 1 says 'Compute advantage Â_i with (α, β) and X_i' but the mapping from the posterior to per-response advantages (especially for all-correct/all-incorrect groups, and how this differs from GRPO's normalization) is left implicit. This hurts reproducibility and makes the method's precise departure from GRPO hard to assess from the main paper.

GRPO-DBB uses a different clipping configuration (0.98, 0.98) than all baselines (0.2, 0.28). Although Appendix D provides a convincing control showing GRPO does not benefit from the wider range, each method is reported with its own best hyperparameter, and the main-table comparisons are thus not strictly matched configurations.

The central theoretical claim—that DBB achieves lower MSE than point estimation—is only conditional on unspecified 'mild non-stationarity'; there is no formal condition or theorem delineating when the MSE inequality holds, so the theoretical contribution is largely a bias-variance decomposition verified empirically.

Evaluation is limited to a single training dataset (DAPO-Math-17k) and a single model family (Qwen3), so the generality of the gains across training distributions and model families remains unverified.

The mechanism behind the very large OOD gains (+8-10 Acc@8 over GRPO) is attributed only qualitatively to Bayesian uncertainty modeling; the causal link between estimator MSE and OOD generalization is asserted rather than demonstrated.
λ is tuned per model scale based on validation trends, and no code release is stated, which together with the implicit advantage definition somewhat limits practical reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: recasting group-based advantage computation as reward-distribution estimation and replacing the empirical mean with a per-prompt discounted Beta-Bernoulli posterior is simple, costs essentially nothing in memory or compute, and directly addresses the variance-collapse pathology of GRPO.

The derivations in Sections 3.2-3.3 and Appendices B, H, and I are correct and clearly presented; the shrinkage interpretation (Eq. 14-15) and the decomposition of MSE into bias (historical drift) and variance components are transparent.

The evaluation protocol is more careful than typical RLVR papers: matched total rollout budgets across methods, four evaluation seeds with paired one-sided t-tests per prompt, Acc@8 on six in-distribution and three OOD benchmarks, plus a Best@8 check (Appendix F) showing that reduced training entropy does not come at the cost of exploration diversity.

Appendix D is a commendable, honest effort to isolate the clipping-range confound: it shows GRPO-DBB under the standard clip range degrades while GRPO under the wider range does not improve, which partially rules out the trivial explanation that the gains come from the wider (0.98, 0.98) clip.

Appendices H and I benchmark DBB against sensible alternative shrinkage estimators (EMA, Laplace, empirical Bayes), giving the reader a sense of where the proposed estimator sits among simpler options.
weaknesses: No independent training seeds. All headline results appear to come from a single training run per method; the four 'independent runs' vary only evaluation seeds. RLVR training outcomes are known to vary substantially across training seeds, so the claimed gains of ~2-3.4 in-distribution points may not be distinguishable from training-run variance. The ablation tables (Tables 2, 3, 6) report no standard deviations at all, and the small margins among lambda settings (e.g., 15.47 vs 15.55 on the 0.6B model) could easily be noise.

The discount factor lambda is selected per model scale based on downstream benchmark performance (Section 4.2: lambda = 0.5 for 1.7B, 0.75 for 8B 'empirically selected based on performance trends'), i.e., tuned on the same evaluation benchmarks reported in Table 1. This inflates the headline numbers relative to baselines, which did not receive equivalent per-benchmark tuning, and the 'rule of thumb' linking model scale to lambda is post-hoc.

The per-method clipping configuration is a real confound. The method effectively bundles two changes: DBB estimation and a much wider clip range ((0.98, 0.98) vs (0.2, 0.28)). Appendix D mitigates but does not eliminate this concern; a fairer design would tune the clip range for all methods on a validation set rather than reporting each method with its 'own best configuration,' and ideally would apply DBB and wide clipping as a 2x2 factorial design with training-seed replicates.

The theoretical claim that DBB 'achieves a lower MSE under mild non-stationarity' is never formalized: 'mild non-stationarity' is not defined, no condition is given under which MSE(DBB) < MSE(point) is proven, and Eq. (19) conditions on a fixed trajectory {p_1..p_tau} while Eq. (20) conditions only on p_tau, making the two MSE expressions not directly comparable as stated. The MSE comparison is ultimately empirical, on a single model and dataset.

The mechanism by which DBB produces its gains is under-examined relative to its importance. DBB assigns nonzero (posterior-baseline-based) advantages to zero-variance groups, which is essentially a biased baseline rather than a variance-reduced estimate of the same quantity the point estimator targets. The paper should more rigorously separate 'better estimation of p_tau' (MSE story) from 'different, intentionally biased training signal on zero-variance prompts' (optimization story); the Section 5.1 explanation is plausible but speculative. The exact advantage formula used with (alpha, beta) in Algorithm 1 line 11 is not fully specified in the main text, which hurts reproducibility.

Generality of evidence is thin: one training dataset (DAPO-Math-17k), one model family (Qwen3), and only GRPO/Dr.GRPO as host algorithms. Some results invite scrutiny, e.g., RePO underperforming vanilla GRPO on several benchmarks suggests baseline tuning may be imperfect, and the very large OOD gains (e.g., +16.97 on BBH for 1.7B) are surprising for a change that only alters per-prompt scalar reward statistics and warrant deeper investigation into evaluation artifacts.

Originality is modest: the method is a discounted Beta-Bernoulli conjugate update, i.e., a standard Bayesian technique applied as a per-prompt shrinkage baseline, and its closest competitor (per-prompt EMA, Appendix H) achieves nearly identical minimum MSE (0.0086 vs 0.0083). The paper does not clearly demonstrate why the Beta-Bernoulli parametrization specifically matters beyond this marginal MSE difference.

The limitations discussion is thin: hyperparameter sensitivity to lambda and prior (Appendices E, G) is acknowledged, but the implications of injecting stale historical information (e.g., risk of reinforcing outdated all-correct/all-incorrect patterns as the policy shifts, potential for reward-hacking style pathologies) are not discussed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated reframing of group-based RLVR advantage computation as a statistical estimation problem, connecting variance collapse to the high variance of small-sample point estimators of the Bernoulli reward probability.

The DBB estimator is simple, cheap (no extra memory, no extra forward passes, no changes to sampling), and plug-and-play; the posterior mean provably cannot collapse to zero-variance degenerate values since posterior parameters remain strictly positive.

Solid statistical analysis: the paper derives the conditional expectation, variance, and MSE of the DBB estimator (Appendix B) and correctly characterizes it as an exponentially weighted average of historical reward probabilities with an explicit bias-variance trade-off (Eq. 14-15, Table 4).

Comprehensive and careful empirical evaluation: two model scales (1.7B, 8B), six in-distribution and three out-of-distribution benchmarks, four seeds, paired one-sided t-tests with per-cell p-values, and multiple strong baselines (RePO, GRESO, DAPO, Dr.GRPO) trained under equalized total rollout budgets.

Notably thorough confound control: Appendix D explicitly isolates the effect of the wider clipping range required by DBB (0.98, 0.98 vs 0.2, 0.28) and shows GRPO under the wider range does not improve, ruling out the clip range as the source of gains. This kind of control is often missing in RLVR papers.

Strong ablations: discount factor λ sweeps across three model scales (including 0.6B), prior hyperparameter sensitivity (Appendix E), and comparisons against alternative shrinkage estimators (EMA, Laplace smoothing, empirical Bayes), showing DBB attains the lowest minimum MSE.

The MSE analysis (Section 5.3) is linked to downstream performance, and training dynamics (entropy, response length, Best@8) are examined to argue that lower training entropy does not sacrifice evaluation-time diversity.
Reproducibility is good: standard framework (verl), verifier (Math-Verify), full hyperparameter tables, and clear protocol descriptions.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: discounted Bayesian updating of a conjugate prior is classical (exponential forgetting / discounted posterior methods), and the main contribution is its application to GRPO advantage estimation rather than a new estimation principle. The related-work discussion could better acknowledge this lineage.

The central theoretical claim that DBB achieves lower MSE than point estimation 'under mild non-stationarity' is not established as a formal result; the paper itself concedes the bias-variance comparison 'depends on the relative magnitudes' and verifies it empirically. A condition under which DBB is guaranteed to beat point estimation would strengthen the contribution.

The method introduces a new sensitive hyperparameter (λ) whose optimal value varies by model scale (0.25 for 0.6B, 0.5 for 1.7B, 0.75 for 8B). The proposed rule of thumb is heuristic and extrapolated cautiously; a principled or adaptive choice (acknowledged as future work) is needed for the method to be reliably deployable.
The method is limited to binary verifiable rewards and a single training dataset (DAPO-Math-17k); generalization to dense/process rewards or other domains is only sketched in the conclusion.
The MSE ground truth is itself an empirical mean over 128 extra rollouts, so the estimator-quality conclusions in Section 5.3 inherit some measurement noise; this is acknowledged but not quantified.
There is a presentation flaw: two appendices are both labeled 'E' (prior sensitivity and Mean@8/Best@8 curves), which could confuse readers.

Some interpretive claims (e.g., that lower training entropy reflects 'sharper exploration' rather than a potential exploration deficit) are plausible given the Best@8 results but remain somewhat speculative; the mechanism section mixes observation and interpretation.
